faq.q: Is 350 KB safe under a 400 KB limit?
faq.a: Yes. The file lands at 315–350 KB, about 50 KB under the cap.

faq.q: How long does a 350 KB file take to upload?
faq.a: On a slow 1 Mbps mobile connection, about three seconds. Smaller files help on weak signals, so use the lowest size your form allows.

faq.q: Does a higher KB fix a blurry photo?
faq.a: No. If the original is out of focus, retake it. Extra kilobytes keep the blur exactly as it is.

paras: No exam in our list sets 350 KB as a cap. It is a buffer target: if a form allows up to 400 KB for an image, 350 KB passes with room to spare, even if the portal measures size slightly differently. It also works for detailed scans, such as a full-page marksheet, where you want the most quality a small file can carry.
At 350 KB the JPEG quality is high enough that compression is practically invisible, even on printed tables and stamps. Bigger targets mainly preserve camera noise.

As a rough guide, a passport-style photo on a plain background stays clean at about 720×960 pixels in 350 KB. A busy background or a dim, noisy shot needs more kilobytes for the same size, and a signature on white paper needs far fewer.

Whatever you add, the download is a baseline JPG (not progressive) between 315 and 350 KB. It stays under 3,50,000 bytes, so it passes whether the portal counts 1 KB as 1000 or 1024 bytes, and hidden camera and location data are removed.
Check the format before the size. If the portal says "PDF only", a perfect 350 KB JPG will still be rejected; use Images to PDF for those fields.
Pick the size just under the limit printed on your form. If the form gives both a minimum and a maximum, a range page fills in the minimum for you.
